Introspection. The systematic self-observation and analysis of one's own mental states, thoughts, and feelings. Wilhelm Wundt pioneered this as the primary method of experimental psychology in the nineteenth century, attempting to make consciousness scientifically measurable. While its limitations led to its eclipse by behaviorism, introspection remains important to contemporary cognitive science and phenomenology.

Wundt developed introspection as an experimental method in his psychological laboratory at Leipzig University. The method involved trained observers systematically reporting their immediate conscious experience under controlled stimulus conditions. Wundt believed introspection could measure the elemental contents of consciousness—sensations, feelings, and their combinations. This represented an attempt to make psychology a rigorous natural science by measuring mental phenomena the way physics measures matter. However, the method suffered from poor reliability. Observers' reports could not be easily verified or replicated across individuals. Behaviorists like John B. Watson criticized it severely, arguing that subjective mental reports had no place in science.

While introspection lost its primacy in psychology, it never disappeared entirely. Cognitive psychology later rehabilitated careful introspection combined with objective measurement. Introspection differs from casual self-reflection by requiring systematic training, standard conditions, and careful reporting of immediate experience. Structuralism, the psychological school built on Wundt's introspection, sought to decompose consciousness into basic units like atoms in physics. Modern neuroscience has partially rehabilitated introspective reports as data points that complement brain imaging techniques like fMRI and other objective measures of brain activity. Phenomenology, a philosophical movement, adopted introspection as a rigorous method for studying the structure of conscious experience. Wilhelm Wundt pioneered this work as the foundational psychologist developing introspection as a method. The attempt to make introspection scientifically rigorous shaped psychology as science. The school of structuralism built on introspective analysis of consciousness. Consciousness itself was the phenomenon introspection aimed to study. Empiricism provides the philosophical foundation for introspection as a method. Behaviorism emerged as the movement that rejected introspection in favor of observable behavior. Cognitive science represents the modern field that has reintegrated introspection with objective methods. The think-aloud protocol used in cognitive and usability research is a modern heir to introspection.
